items.text: Functions: one job, clear name, return the result
Classes bundle data and behaviour; `@dataclass` for data-heavy classes
Catch specific exceptions, raise meaningful ones, read tracebacks bottom-up

captions.text: In the last lesson you learned how to hold data.
Now you will learn how to organise the code that works on it.
Functions give logic a name, classes bundle data with behaviour, and exceptions let
your program fail clearly and recover safely.
Agents call tools that fail all the time, so this last part matters a lot.
You will write functions with parameters, default values, and return values.
Avoid a classic bug that can leak data between users.
Create your own classes, and the shorter dataclasses.
And handle, raise, and define your own exceptions, and read a traceback calmly.
A function is a named, reusable block of code.
You define it once, and call it as often as you like.
The def keyword starts a function.
Inside the parentheses are its parameters, the inputs.
The text in triple quotes is a docstring, describing what it does.
And return sends the result back to whoever called it.
You can pass arguments by position, or by name, as keyword arguments.
Keywords make calls with several numbers much easier to read.
Notice the underscores in two million.
Python ignores them.
They are just there for readability.
This second function has a default value.
If the caller does not pass max words, it uses eight.
It returns early when the text is already short enough.
Otherwise it keeps the first words and adds an ellipsis.
Here we call it three times: once with a long sentence, once with a short one, and
once overriding the default.
The costs come back as plain numbers, the long sentence is shortened, and the last
call keeps only two words.
Give each function one job, and name it with a verb, like estimate cost or load
records.
Return results instead of printing them.
Then the caller decides what to do, and you can test the function easily.
Use keyword arguments whenever a call would otherwise be a mystery list of numbers.
And never use a mutable default, like an empty list.
Let me show you why.
This function stores chat history.
The default empty list looks harmless, but Python creates it only once, when the
function is defined.
Every call that uses the default shares that same list.
So Alice sends a message, then Bob sends one, and Bob's history contains Alice's
message.
In an AI app, that is a privacy bug: one user's conversation leaking into another's.
The fix is the standard Python pattern.
Default to None, and create a fresh list inside the function.
The output proves it.
With the buggy version, Bob sees Alice's message.
With the fixed version, each call starts clean.
Now, classes.
Functions organise behaviour.
Classes organise data together with the behaviour that belongs to it.
A class is a blueprint.
It describes what every object of that kind has, and what it can do.
An object, also called an instance, is one real thing built from that blueprint.
You can create as many as you like.
Attributes are the data stored on each object.
And methods are functions that belong to the class and work on that object's data.
Here is a Conversation class.
The special dunder init method runs whenever a new object is created.
Its first parameter, self, is the object being built, so self dot messages stores a
list on that particular object.
Add and last are methods.
They also take self first, so they can read and change this object's messages.
Methods with double underscores plug your class into Python itself.
Defining dunder len makes the built-in len function work on a conversation.
Creating an object looks like calling a function.
We add two messages, then print the length and the last message.
A second conversation is a completely separate object, with its own list.
Three messages in the first conversation, and just the system message in the other.
Many classes in AI code mostly hold data: a model configuration, a usage record, a
tool result.
For those, Python's dataclass decorator writes the boring parts for you.
You just list the fields, with their types and optional defaults.
The decorator generates the init method, a readable print form, and equality
comparison.
Notice the stop field.
Remember the mutable default bug?
Dataclasses protect you from it: for a list default, you must use field with a
default factory.
Creating objects, printing one, and comparing two with the same values, which counts
as equal.
The generated print form shows every field, and the equality check is True.
In the project, our usage record is a dataclass.
Now, exceptions.
When something goes wrong, Python raises an exception.
If nothing handles it, the program stops.
Put code that might fail inside a try block.
Converting text to a number fails if the text isn't a number.
The except block runs only if that specific error happens.
Here we handle a value error by reporting it and returning zero.
The else block runs only when the try block succeeded.
And finally always runs, whether things went well or not.
That makes it the right place for cleanup, like closing a connection.
Look at the order.
For one twenty, the finally message prints before the value, because finally runs on
the way out of the function.
For a b c, the error is handled, finally still runs, and we get zero.
You can define your own exceptions by inheriting from Exception.
A base class for your project, with more specific ones below it, is a great pattern.
The raise statement stops the function immediately and hands the problem to the
caller.
A negative cost is a programming error, so that's a value error.
Going over budget is a business rule, so it gets our own budget exceeded error.
The caller catches only budget exceeded, and stops charging.
Agents need exactly this kind of guard, a hard spending limit, which we'll build
properly in Module 7.
The first two charges succeed, and the third is refused with a clear message.
On the left is a pattern you must avoid.
A bare except with pass hides every error, including bugs in your own code.
The program carries on with no result, and you have no idea why.
On the right, you catch only the error you expect and know how to handle.
Anything unexpected still surfaces, so you can see it and fix it.
When an exception isn't handled, Python prints a traceback.
It looks scary, but read it from the bottom up.
The last line is the error: a key error for the key model.
The lines above it show the path the program took, with the most recent call last.
Here, the failing line is config, model, inside get model, called from start agent.
So the fix is to make sure the configuration contains a model, or to read it with
get and a default.
Quick check.
Why is a function with history equals an empty list as a default dangerous?
Because the default list is created once and shared by every call that uses it.
Default to None and create a fresh list inside the function.
Functions do one job, have a clear name, and return their result.
Default mutable arguments to None.
Classes bundle data and behaviour, and dataclasses make data-heavy classes short.
Catch specific exceptions, raise meaningful ones, and read tracebacks from the
bottom up.
Next, you will split code across files and packages, and work with files, JSON, and
environment variables.
